extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for when acts by licensees, purchasers, carriers, contractors, agents, employees, and third parties constitute patent infringement; and principles for infringement of combination patents (elements and equivalents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee exceeding licensed scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who acts outside the territory or period for which his license has been granted, or in any other way exceeds the power conferred upon him, is guilty of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: using the invention outside the licensed territory or after the license period ends. An assignee of an assignable license rests under the same limitations as the original licensee and may infringe by the same modes of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee doing acts not authorized by license
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee violating the terms of his license by doing acts not authorized thereby at once infringes the patent and breaks his contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include selling outside a permitted territory or performing unauthorized uses; such acts give rise to both contract and infringement remedies (see Pope Mfg. Co. v. Owsley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee making articles different from patent description not protected by license
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to make the article described in the patent does not protect a licensee who makes one different from the one described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the licensee makes a different article (not within the described claim), he is not insulated from infringement liability (see Miller's Falls Co. v. Ives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to pay royalties is not per se infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee merely refusing to pay his royalties cannot be treated as an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonpayment is a contract breach but does not automatically convert the licensee's use into patent infringement (see Seibert Cylinder Oil-Cup Co. v. Detroit Lubricator Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee exceeding quantity limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee infringes if he exceeds the number of patented articles covered by his license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a license to use/make a specified number of machines; using more than the allowed number is infringement (see Aspinwall Mfg. Co. v. Gill).

rubrics_metrics.name: License covenants cannot bar infringement defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenants in a license cannot deprive the licensee of the right to show that his acts do not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractual waivers cannot foreclose a showing that the acts fall outside the patent claim (see White v. Lee).

rubrics_metrics.name: License under one patent does not protect against another patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A license under one patent affords no protection against liability for infringement of a different patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding a license under Patent A does not immunize use that infringes Patent B (see Stuart v. Shantz; Blanchard v. Putnam).

rubrics_metrics.name: License to use does not include right to make or sell
rubrics_metrics.description: A license granting the right to use the patented article does not give the licensee the right to make or sell it unless expressly included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'license to use' vs 'license to make or sell' — different rights and limits (see Aiken v. Manchester Print Works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee selling components to known non-licensees is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee authorized to sell materials to be used in a patented process infringes by selling to others who are known not to be licensees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge that purchaser will use the materials infringingly converts the sale into contributory/participatory infringement (see Willis v. McCullen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicing an independent infringing invention under cover of a license
rubrics_metrics.description: If a licensee practices his own infringing invention under cover of the license, he is an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the license as a pretext to practice a separate invention that itself infringes is actionable (see Miller's Falls Co. v. Ives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of machines in excess of permitted configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of two machines in succession under a license to use one is an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where license limits number/configuration, departure constitutes infringement (see Bloomer v. Gilpin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-use of a marked article may be permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an infringement to use a second time an article marked 'Licensed to use once only' in certain cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific statutory or case exceptions may allow re-use; see American Cotton Tie Co. v. Simmons for context and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser from rightful seller has implied license to use
rubrics_metrics.description: The purchaser of a patented article from one who had a right to sell it may use it for any purpose and in any place until it is destroyed, unless purchase terms provide otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But such purchaser cannot reconstruct the article or make a new one in its stead without infringing; conditional sales may limit implied license (see Metropolitan Washing Mach. Co. v. Earle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser from infringing seller acquires no license
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser from an infringing seller acquires no license to use the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if compensated, wrongful sellers cannot convey a patent license to buyers (see Gilbert & Barker Mfg. Co. v. Bussing). Exceptions when owner is compensated for wrongful sale may create an implied license to the purchaser (Steam Stone Cutter Co. v. Sheldon; Allis v. Stowell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser with knowledge of prior grants cannot use within granted territory
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser of articles with knowledge of prior grants cannot use the articles within the granted territory of a prior grantee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of existing exclusive grants limits the purchaser's permitted use and resale (see Sheldon Axle Co. v. Standard Axle Works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license by acquiescence/compensation/permission
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who acquiesces in another's practice of the invention, receiving compensation or the promise of compensation, or who permits construction before grant, impliedly licenses the acts so acquiesced in; the scope is determined by past conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied licenses arise by contract or estoppel; their limits follow the actual enjoyment/usage and may permit continued use until the article ceases to exist but not reconstruction or replacement with new articles (see Blanchard v. Sprague; Seibert Cylinder Oil-Cup Co. v. Detroit Lubricator Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer's implied license for employee-invented improvements applied to business
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee who applies his invention to the employer's business and annexes it to employer apparatus confers on the employer a license which neither he nor his assignees can revoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers gain a right to use inventions incorporated into their property during employment; rebuilding or repurposing beyond that authority may be infringement (see Herman v. Herman; Continental Windmill Co. v. Empire Windmill Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defective patent consent-based constructions and re-issue/extension rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who constructed the invention with the inventor's consent under a defective patent may use it after a re-issue or extension to the extent permitted by the prior use (but replacing with new ones or reconstruction may be infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use before amendment does not create blanket rights under amended patents; statutory and case law (e.g., Rev. Stat. §4899) limit scope (see McWilliams Mfg. Co. v. Blundell; Wade v. Metcalf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on implied license after assignment/extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee publicly authorized all persons to use his invention under the original term, those who used it may continue to use what they had on hand during an extension, but implied licenses do not grant a right to make new articles beyond that scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignees of original term may use existing articles but have no implied license to make them for new purposes; scope determined by conduct and terms (see Wooster v. Sklenbeig).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by common carriers when willful/colusive
rubrics_metrics.description: A common carrier may be held to participate in infringing acts and be enjoined if it conspires with an infringing manufacturer to transport products or otherwise willfully aids the infringing sale or use — ordinary carriage without illegitimate intent does not make the carrier liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability often depends on notice and collusion; carriers who transport infringing goods after due notice may be treated as agents of the infringer and subject to injunction unless they disclose shippers (see American Cotton Tie Co. v. McCready).

rubrics_metrics.name: Import/customs agents without possession/control not liable
rubrics_metrics.description: Importation and transshipment by customs-house agents who have no possession or control of infringing articles does not make them liable for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability requires possession/control or willful participation; mere routine customs functions are insufficient (see Nobel's Explosives Co. v. Jones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor's liability for performing infringing work
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor who, in fulfilling obligations, violates a patent is answerable for infringement; foreknowledge that work will infringe imposes a duty to procure a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If entered into in ignorance of the patent, contractor still may be liable though ignorance can affect damages and relief; public-interest contracts may be allowed to finish with patentee compensated afterward (see Jacobs v. Commissioners of Hamilton Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agents and workmen who voluntarily participate are infringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents who voluntarily participate in an infringing act become infringers themselves, even if they have no pecuniary interest; mere agents acting under orders and without choice typically do not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salesmen receiving commissions or servants deriving independent benefit may incur separate liability; workmen obeying orders and exercising no choice generally are not liable (see cases cited under §920–§921).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private individual voluntary makers/users are infringers regardless of motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Private individuals who voluntarily engage in unauthorized manufacture, use, or sale of the patented invention are guilty of infringement; motive and knowledge are immaterial for liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The outer act (manufacture/use/sale) is determinative; specific intent or culpability is irrelevant unless a particular statute or doctrine requires intent (see §921 and cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patent identity and infringement test
rubrics_metrics.description: A patented combination's identity depends on the presence in the combination of each of the claimed elements (or their equivalents) and upon their co-operation in the specific manner to produce the ultimate result; infringement requires making, using, or selling a combination in which precisely the same elements or their equivalents are united under the same co-operative law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of an element, a different number/character/mode of cooperation, or a differently combined set of elements generally creates a different invention and is not infringement unless equivalents supply omitted features (see §922 and authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalents in combination patents may produce infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is infringed if equivalents of claimed elements are used in the same plan of cooperation; courts ask whether an omitted part is supplied by an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an omitted element is replaced by an equivalent performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve the same result, infringement may be found (see Water Meter Co. v. Desper; Dederick v. Whitman Agricultural Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different arrangement or new combination may or may not infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: A different combination of the same elements, or a union of different mechanical devices accomplishing the same result, is generally not an infringement of the original combination patent unless the plan of cooperation and essential character are substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting elements from distinct patented combinations and uniting them into a third does not ordinarily invade either; however, a change of arrangement may still be infringement in some cases (see Rowell v. Lindsay; Belle Patent Button Fastener Co. v. Lucas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using less than all elements of a combination usually not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of less than all the elements of a patented combination does not infringe the combination patent alone, unless the omitted element is supplied by an equivalent or some other legal theory applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the defendant's device supplies the function of the omitted element by an equivalent; merely performing the same overall result by a different combination typically falls outside the combination claim (cases: Byerly v. Cleveland Linseed Oil Works; Newark Mach. Co. decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of a new element performing same function may avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendants substitute an element which is new (not known at the date of the complainant's patent) or which performs a substantially different function, they may not infringe the combination patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critical inquiry is whether the substitute is a proper equivalent at the patent's date; a substitute that is novel or that makes a substantially different-functioning machine tends to avoid infringement (see quoted passage in Rowell v. Lindsay and follow-ups).
